title: Traversing the Satisfaction-Diversity Frontier in Text-to-Image Diffusion

paper.title: Traversing the Satisfaction-Diversity Frontier in Text-to-Image Diffusion
paper.abstract: Abstract Text-to-image generation enables users to explore several images generated from the same prompt. For these generated images to be useful, each one must reflect the user’s preferences, measured by a learned reward, and differ visually from the others to maintain diversity. Existing methods are limited: they either address reward and diversity separately or combine them in one aggregate score, enabling high diversity to offset low rewards. In this paper, we address these limitations by formulating generation as satisficing : every image (candidate) must satisfy a reward floor and the batch of images must satisfy a diversity cutoff. The reward floor controls the balance between worst-candidate reward and batch diversity; we show that varying this floor defines a Pareto frontier. To traverse this frontier, we introduce SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method. SatisDive uses a batch-relative reward cutoff to distinguish lower- from higher-reward candidates, emphasizing reward improvement for candidates below the cutoff and diversity among candidates above it. On Pick-a-Pic, at matched DreamSim, SatisDive improves worst-candidate reward over FK steering by up to 0.43 0.43 with FLUX.1-dev as the base model and HPSv3 as the reward, and by up to 0.70 0.70 with SANA-1.6B as the base model and ImageReward as the reward. More broadly, across their overlapping DreamSim ranges, SatisDive’s satisfaction–diversity curve Pareto-dominates FK steering’s curve in each setting.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: An important goal of text-to-image generation is to give users a choice among several high-quality candidate images. For example, a user creating a poster illustration may compare images generated from the same prompt, choosing the lighting, background, or composition that best fits the poster. Recent inference-time methods increase diversity ( Singh et al., 2024 ) to provide a wider range of options, maximize a learned reward ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) to align generated images with user preferences, or select images by maximizing a linear combination of total image reward and batch diversity ( Parmar et al., 2026 ) . However, these approaches can still limit the user’s viable choices. Firstly, reward-steering methods can concentrate sampling on higher-reward images, making the returned images visually similar ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Shekhar et al., 2026 ) . Secondly, reward-free diversity methods make generated images more visually different, but do not explicitly account for learned reward ( Singh et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Corso et al., 2024 ; Vinograd et al., 2026 ) . Thirdly, batch-level reward–diversity objectives ( Parmar et al., 2026 ) allow greater diversity or high rewards for other images to compensate for one image’s low reward. These limitations motivate controlling worst-image reward through a reward floor, i.e., a minimum reward level required of each candidate. As the reward floor increases, the batch can become less diverse since fewer images satisfy the floor. We show that varying the reward floor defines a Pareto frontier between worst-image reward and batch diversity, which we call the satisfaction–diversity frontier. Along this frontier, we formulate image generation as satisficing ( Simon, 1956 ) : every generated image must satisfy a reward floor, and the batch must satisfy a diversity cutoff. Once a candidate clears the reward floor, further increases in reward do not improve satisfaction. To this end, we introduce SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method. As Figure 1 shows, SatisDive generates visually distinct images above the reward floor, while FK steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) , a strong reward-steering baseline, returns nearly identical images. Figure 1: SatisDive returns four visually distinct images above the reward floor, while FK steering returns four nearly identical images. We use the SANA-1.6B ( Xie et al., 2025 ) flow matching model with ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) reward model. On a Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) prompt depicting two colliding viruses, the minimum reward is 0.66 0.66 for FK steering and 1.25 1.25 for SatisDive, with reward floor ρ = 1.19 \rho{=}1.19 . Our objective traverses the satisfaction–diversity frontier through a per-image reward penalty and a batch-level diversity penalty. Under the satisficing formulation, a visually different but low-reward image should contribute less to batch diversity. Thus, these penalties are complementary: images with rewards below a batch-relative reward cutoff incur larger reward penalties and contribute less to the diversity penalty, and images with rewards above the cutoff incur smaller reward penalties but contribute more to the diversity penalty. Because some candidates may remain low reward throughout denoising, we introduce late-stage latent replacement, which replaces their latents with those of higher-reward candidates. Subsequent stochastic denoising and the diversity penalty allow the resulting trajectories to produce distinct images. Empirically, SatisDive improves worst-candidate reward without sacrificing batch diversity: across their overlapping DreamSim ranges, SatisDive’s worst-candidate reward is consistently higher than FK steering’s, thus our satisfaction–diversity curves Pareto-dominate FK steering’s on both FLUX and SANA. Our contributions are as follows. • We show that different reward floors define a Pareto frontier between worst-image reward and batch diversity. Under our satisficing formulation, every image must satisfy the selected reward floor, and the batch must satisfy a diversity cutoff. • We introduce SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method whose objective provably traverses this satisfaction–diversity frontier. The objective uses a batch-relative reward cutoff to emphasize reward improvement for lower-reward candidates and diversity among higher-reward candidates. • At matched DreamSim, SatisDive improves worst-image reward by up to 0.43 0.43 on FLUX and 0.70 0.70 on SANA. Our satisfaction–diversity curve Pareto-dominates the curves traced by FK steering on the FLUX.1-dev and SANA-1.6B base models.

sections.heading: 2 Problem Formulation
sections.text: A rectified-flow text-to-image model ( Liu et al., 2023 ) generates an image from a prompt c c using a learned velocity field v θ ​ ( x t , t , c ) v_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c) . This formulation also covers other diffusion models such as DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , which differ in their noise schedule ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . Table 4 in Appendix A summarizes the notation used throughout the paper. Let p θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ c ) p_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid c) denote the base model’s distribution. We consider methods that maintain K K candidates throughout a single sampling pass and generate a batch of K K images (denoted x 0 1 : K x_{0}^{1:K} ). Given a reward r ⁡ ( x 0 , c ) r(x_{0},c) , we first consider reward-steering methods (e.g., FK steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) ) that yield high-reward images by targeting the tilted distribution p λ p_{\lambda} : p λ ​ ( x 0 ∣ c ) ∝ p θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ c ) ​ exp ⁡ ( λ ​ r ​ ( x 0 , c ) ) , λ ≥ 0 , p_{\lambda}(x_{0}\mid c)\propto p_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid c)\,\exp\!\big(\lambda\,r(x_{0},c)\big),\qquad\lambda\geq 0, (1) where larger λ \lambda increases the relative probability of higher-reward images. These methods approximate Eq. 1 by resampling candidate latents at intermediate timesteps with selection probabilities determined by candidate rewards; these rewards are evaluated on the model’s estimate x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} of the final image, computed as: x ^ 0 = x t − σ t ​ v θ ​ ( x t , t , c ) , \hat{x}_{0}=x_{t}-\sigma_{t}v_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c), (2) where σ t \sigma_{t} is the noise level at timestep t t . Since rectified flow is deterministic, these steering methods use the equivalent marginal-preserving stochastic form ( Mark et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Limitations of current methods.
sections.text: The reward-only tilt in Eq. 1 weights each candidate’s selection probability during resampling according to its reward, without considering how the K K images differ. Proposition 1 (proof in Appendix B ) states what happens when this tilt is applied to the current candidates during resampling. Proposition 1 ( As λ → ∞ \lambda\to\infty , resampling produces K K copies of the highest-reward candidate ) . At a resampling step with a unique highest-reward candidate, increasing λ \lambda increases its expected number of copies. In the limit as λ → ∞ \lambda\to\infty , the probability that all K K resampled candidates are copies of the highest-reward candidate approaches one. Consequently, a greater reward tilt can reduce the number of distinct candidates retained after resampling and thereby reduce the visual diversity among the generated images. A second class of methods increases the diversity of generated images. NegToMe ( Singh et al., 2024 ) , for instance, increases the distance between the candidates’ features. Being reward-agnostic, these methods do not constrain the sampling distribution toward higher rewards. Figure 2 visualizes the limitations of reward-steering and diversity methods in a toy 2D setting (details in Appendix C.1 ). Figure 2: In a toy setting, each baseline tends towards high diversity or high reward, not both. Each method generates K = 4 K{=}4 candidates from a frozen flow model trained on a mixture of Gaussians (details in Appendix C.1 ). Reward is bounded in ( 0 , 1 ] (0,1] , and the midpoint ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 is a reward floor that every candidate must satisfy. (a) To visualize clearly the coverage of high-reward regions, candidates are 2D points on a Cartesian x x – y y grid rather than images. We show one selected illustrative batch of K = 4 K{=}4 candidates per method. DAS’s candidates are all above ρ \rho but are not diverse; they cover only a single high-reward region (yellow circles). Conversely, NegToMe’s candidates are diverse yet are all below ρ \rho (red circles). In these batches, only ours has all candidates above ρ \rho in distinct high-reward regions. (b) We plot worst-candidate reward against diversity (mean pairwise distance) averaged over 200 runs for each method. Methods in the shaded green region have average worst-candidate rewards greater than ρ \rho . DAS achieves the highest reward but lowest diversity; NegToMe achieves the highest diversity but lowest reward. A natural third alternative treats diversity as a second reward and samples from a joint tilt: π joint ( x 0 1 : K ∣ c ) ∝ ∏ k = 1 K p θ ( x 0 k ∣ c ) exp ( λ ∑ k = 1 K r ( x 0 k , c ) + μ D ( x 0 1 : K ) ) , λ , μ ≥ 0 , \pi_{\mathrm{joint}}(x_{0}^{1:K}\mid c)\propto\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_{\theta}(x_{0}^{k}\mid c)\,\exp\!\Big(\lambda\sum_{k=1}^{K}r(x_{0}^{k},c)+\mu D(x_{0}^{1:K})\Big),\qquad\lambda,\mu\geq 0, (3) where D D is a batch-level diversity term and μ \mu weights it against reward r r . Because reward and diversity are aggregated, the joint objective can be gamed: for λ > 0 \lambda>0 , one unit of D D offsets a decrease of μ / λ \mu/\lambda in total reward. This exchange exists for every positive μ \mu , so π joint \pi_{\mathrm{joint}} never requires a candidate to be high-reward.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: The approaches discussed in Section 2 do not jointly require a reward floor for every candidate and a minimum diversity for the whole batch. We therefore formulate generation as satisficing ( Simon, 1956 ) : every candidate must satisfy a reward floor ρ \rho , while the batch must satisfy a diversity requirement. These requirements define the target distribution π ⋆ ( x 0 1 : K ∣ c ) ∝ ( ∏ k = 1 K p θ ( x 0 k ∣ c ) 1 [ r ( x 0 k , c ) ≥ ρ ] ) 1 [ D ( x 0 1 : K ) ≥ δ ] , \pi^{\star}(x_{0}^{1:K}\mid c)\;\propto\;\Big(\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_{\theta}(x_{0}^{k}\mid c)\,\mathbf{1}[r(x_{0}^{k},c)\geq\rho]\Big)\,\mathbf{1}[D(x_{0}^{1:K})\geq\delta], (4) where D D measures batch diversity, δ \delta is the required diversity level, and each indicator equals one when its condition holds and zero otherwise. Rejection sampling would draw K K candidates independently from p θ p_{\theta} and reject the entire batch if either requirement is violated. Because the probability that all K K candidates satisfy the reward floor decreases exponentially with K K , rejection sampling can be prohibitively expensive. We thus introduce SatisDive, which replaces both indicators with differentiable penalties. Our training-free approach rests on two mechanisms: (1) a satisficing objective that increases low rewards and diversifies the batch; and (2) late-stage latent replacement, which replaces the latent of a low-reward candidate with that of a higher-reward candidate. Section 3.1 details the objective and late-stage latent replacement and connects our objective to π ⋆ \pi^{\star} , while Section 3.2 proves that this objective traces the satisfaction–diversity Pareto frontier.

sections.heading: 3.2 SatisDive’s Objective Traces the Satisfaction–Diversity Pareto Frontier
sections.text: By sweeping Δ \Delta , SatisDive’s objective traces a Pareto frontier between reward and diversity. Let A ρ = { x : r ⁡ ( x , c ) ≥ ρ } A_{\rho}=\{x:r(x,c)\geq\rho\} be the set of images that satisfy the floor, and let p ρ p_{\rho} be the base output distribution restricted to A ρ A_{\rho} , preserving relative probabilities within this set. Because the reward constraint applies separately to each candidate, we rewrite π ⋆ \pi^{\star} as a product of K K reward-restricted distributions and the batch diversity indicator: π ⋆ ( x 1 : K ∣ c ) ∝ ( ∏ k = 1 K p ρ ( x k ) ) 1 [ D ( x 1 : K ) ≥ δ ] , p ρ ( x ) ∝ p θ ( x ∣ c ) 1 [ x ∈ A ρ ] . \pi^{\star}(x^{1:K}\mid c)\propto\Big(\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_{\rho}(x^{k})\Big)\,\mathbf{1}[D(x^{1:K})\geq\delta],\qquad p_{\rho}(x)\propto p_{\theta}(x\mid c)\,\mathbf{1}[x\in A_{\rho}]. (10) We denote { p ρ } \{p_{\rho}\} as the family of distributions obtained by varying the reward floor ρ \rho . For each floor, Lemma 5 (Appendix B ) shows two properties of p ρ p_{\rho} . First, among all distributions that assign probability one to A ρ A_{\rho} , p ρ p_{\rho} uniquely minimizes the KL \mathrm{KL} divergence to the base model. Second, the support of every such distribution with finite KL \mathrm{KL} is contained in the support of p ρ p_{\rho} . Every candidate drawn from p ρ p_{\rho} has reward at least ρ \rho . For any two such reward floors ρ ′ \rho^{\prime} and ρ \rho with ρ ′ ≥ ρ \rho^{\prime}\geq\rho , p ρ ′ p_{\rho^{\prime}} has diversity at most that of p ρ p_{\rho} . For each ρ \rho , no distribution over A ρ A_{\rho} at finite KL to p θ p_{\theta} is more diverse than p ρ p_{\rho} . Therefore, { p ρ } \{p_{\rho}\} forms the satisfaction–diversity Pareto frontier among distributions with finite guaranteed reward and finite KL to p θ p_{\theta} . The theorem applies to diversity measures satisfying the stated support-restriction assumption; our experiments evaluate the practical satisfaction–diversity tradeoff using mean pairwise DreamSim. Thus, varying λ \lambda traces { p λ } \{p_{\lambda}\} rather than the satisfaction–diversity Pareto frontier established by { p ρ } \{p_{\rho}\} .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Models, datasets, and baselines. We show results with three frozen base models: FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) , SANA-1.6B ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , and Stable Diffusion 1.5 (SD1.5) ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . We use two reward models, HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , and evaluate on the Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and HPDv2 ( Wu et al., 2023b ) datasets. Our main baselines fall into two categories: 1) reward-steering methods, namely Feynman–Kac (FK) steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) , VASR ( Shekhar et al., 2026 ) , and DAS ( Kim et al., 2025b ) ; and 2) diversity methods, namely Negative Token Merging (NegToMe) ( Singh et al., 2024 ) , which repels candidates in feature space. We also evaluate FK+NegToMe, which combines FK steering with NegToMe’s diversity mechanism. All methods use the same seeds and return K = 4 K{=}4 images (i.e., candidates) per prompt. We report SGI ( Parmar et al., 2026 ) separately in Appendix D.9 because it prunes a much larger pool of 128 128 candidates. Baselines use their recommended settings; sampling details are provided in Appendix C . Metrics. We evaluate images on two axes: reward and diversity. On the reward axis, every method is scored against a reward floor ρ \rho . Rather than choosing ρ \rho arbitrarily, we set it to the base model’s median reward over all prompts. We report worst-candidate reward min k ⁡ r k \min_{k}r_{k} , averaged over prompts, since a batch satisfies the floor ρ \rho precisely when min k ⁡ r k ≥ ρ \min_{k}r_{k}\geq\rho ; we also report mean reward. We define the satisfaction rate SAT ρ \mathrm{SAT}_{\rho} as the fraction of generated candidates whose reward is at least ρ \rho : SAT ρ = 1 N ⋅ K ∑ i = 1 N ⋅ K [ r i ≥ ρ ] , \mathrm{SAT}_{\rho}\;=\;\frac{1}{N\cdot K}\sum_{i=1}^{N\cdot K}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\,r_{i}\geq\rho\,\right], (11) where r i r_{i} is the reward of the i i -th generated candidate and 𝟏 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathbf{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function. N N is the number of prompts, with K K candidates per prompt. Since ρ \rho is the median reward of the base model’s outputs, SAT ρ = 0.5 \mathrm{SAT}_{\rho}\!=\!0.5 indicates parity with the base model. On the diversity axis, each batch is measured by the mean pairwise DreamSim ( Fu et al., 2023 ) and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) among its K K candidates. We additionally report PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) as a held-out reward, which indicates whether reward gains reflect a broader improvement in preference.

sections.heading: 4.1 SatisDive Traverses the Satisfaction–Diversity Frontier
sections.text: Sweeping the tolerance Δ \Delta of our satisficing objective (Eq. 9 ) traces a frontier curve between worst-candidate reward and diversity. As shown in Figure 3 on FLUX and SANA, baseline methods tend to exhibit either high worst-candidate reward but low diversity (DAS, VASR), or low worst-candidate reward and high diversity (NegToMe). Although varying FK steering’s reward-tilt parameter λ \lambda also traces a reward–diversity curve, SatisDive’s curve Pareto-dominates ( Hwang and Masud, 2012 ) FK steering’s over their common DreamSim ranges. sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Reward-driven sampling. Existing methods increase reward through resampling ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2023a ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Shekhar et al., 2026 ) , value-based lookahead ( Li et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) , stochastic transitions ( Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) , adaptive model evaluation ( Kim et al., 2025a ) , or noise-space optimization and regularization ( Hwang et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Harrington et al., 2026 ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) . These methods do not explicitly optimize batch diversity and may collapse candidate lineages ( Shekhar et al., 2026 ) . CREPE ( He et al., 2026 ) uses replica exchange to preserve diversity under reward tilting (comparison in Appendix D.8 ), while SGI ( Parmar et al., 2026 ) selects a reward–diversity batch from a large candidate pool; neither imposes a reward floor on every candidate. Reward-free diversity. NegToMe ( Singh et al., 2024 ) , CNO ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , Particle Guidance ( Corso et al., 2024 ) , and EDDY ( Vinograd et al., 2026 ) repel candidates in feature or prediction space. Other methods vary conditioning, intermediate features, or initial noise ( Sadat et al., 2024 ; Yadav et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , while general guidance modifies model predictions, attention, or guidance schedules ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ; Hong, 2024 ; Karras et al., 2024 ; Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2023 ) . These methods increase diversity without imposing a reward floor. Pareto and satisficing objectives. AIG ( Jena et al., 2025 ) studies average reward against distributional coverage; PROUD ( Yao et al., 2024 ) defines Pareto objectives over per-image properties; and ParetoSlider ( Golan et al., 2026 ) , constrained diffusion alignment ( Khalafi et al., 2025 ) , and SITAlign ( Chehade et al., 2025 ) optimize expected rewards. In contrast, our training-free formulation imposes a reward floor on every candidate and a diversity requirement on the batch, producing a frontier between worst-candidate reward and batch diversity.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: SatisDive formulates image generation as satisficing: every candidate must satisfy a reward floor, and the batch must satisfy a diversity cutoff. Varying the floor provably traces a satisfaction–diversity Pareto frontier. On FLUX.1-dev with HPSv3 and SANA-1.6B with ImageReward, SatisDive’s curves Pareto-dominate FK steering’s over their overlapping DreamSim ranges, improving worst-candidate reward at matched DreamSim by up to 0.43 0.43 and 0.70 0.70 , respectively. Extending the formulation to multiple reward floors remains future work.

sections.heading: Sampling and update schedules.
sections.text: The main comparisons use 499 499 Pick-a-Pic prompts and 3200 3200 HPDv2 prompts; the 200 200 DrawBench prompts are evaluated separately in Appendix D . We compute 95 % 95\% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals by resampling prompts with replacement, keeping each prompt’s four candidates together and holding ρ \rho fixed. The displayed ± \pm values are the interval half-widths. For the reward gaps at matched DreamSim in Figure 3 , we linearly interpolate FK steering’s worst-candidate reward between adjacent evaluated points, without extrapolating beyond its sampled DreamSim range. We sample FLUX at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 with 28 Euler steps and guidance 3.5 3.5 , SANA at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 with 20 Euler steps and guidance 4.5 4.5 , and SD1.5 at 512 × 512 512\times 512 with 100 DDIM ( Song et al., 2021 ) steps, η = 1 \eta=1 , and guidance 7.5 7.5 . For FLUX and SANA, every method uses the marginal-preserving SDE of Mark et al. (2025) with noise amplitude a = 0.3 a=0.3 . At steps where reward is evaluated, we estimate x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} by averaging the velocity predictions from the current and previous steps. Because the SDE correction is applied through a first-order Euler update, we replace SANA’s shipped second-order solver with Euler for each method. For methods with scheduled scoring or resampling, the common steps are 4 , 8 , … , 24 4,8,\dots,24 on FLUX and 3 , 6 , … , 18 3,6,\dots,18 on SANA. On SD1.5, the baselines use their published configurations, and SatisDive follows FK steering’s schedule, updating latents at steps 20 , 40 , 60 , 80 20,40,60,80 and 99 99 . We used an NVIDIA A100 GPU for the original experiments and NVIDIA H100 GPUs for runtime and memory profiling. Unless stated otherwise, each method returns four candidates per prompt using matched starting seeds.

sections.heading: Baseline settings.
sections.text: DAS uses Srinivasan Sampling Process (SSP) resampling, while FK steering uses multinomial resampling; both resample when the effective sample size is below 0.5 ​ K 0.5K . For DAS, the annealing rate γ \gamma is determined by the number of sampling steps, and we set α \alpha using its recommended range for the ratio of the reward-guidance norm to the model-drift norm. FK steering applies e λ ​ r e^{\lambda r} to the unstandardized reward, so we select λ \lambda according to the reward scale. We use the published NegToMe settings.

sections.heading: SatisDive settings.
sections.text: We use a fixed step-size multiplier of 1 1 for the latent updates. We set δ \delta to the median of the ( K 2 ) \binom{K}{2} pairwise distances at the first update step and set β d = 1 2 ​ δ \beta_{d}=\tfrac{1}{2}\delta . At each update, the diversity D D in Eq. 8 is the mean of the current pairwise distances weighted by q i ​ q j q_{i}q_{j} . Each d i ​ j d_{ij} is the cosine distance between pooled features from FLUX joint block 12, SANA transformer block 7, or the SD1.5 UNet bottleneck. We apply late-stage latent replacement only during the second half of denoising ( s > T / 2 s>T/2 ) for every reward and base-model setting. We recompute τ \tau at each update step but stop gradients through max k ⁡ r k \max_{k}r_{k} ; otherwise, increasing the current maximum reward would raise τ \tau and increase the penalties on the other candidates, producing a gradient that reduces the maximum reward. The only SatisDive setting swept in the main experiments is the tolerance Δ \Delta . For each reward and base model, the selected Δ \Delta is approximately three-quarters of the median per-prompt difference between the largest and smallest candidate rewards. We also report sweeps over Δ \Delta .

sections.heading: Numerical latent updates.
sections.text: For each candidate, we normalize the reward and diversity gradients separately. We weight the normalized reward gradient by ( 1 − q k ) / max j ⁡ ( 1 − q j ) (1-q_{k})/\max_{j}(1-q_{j}) , then clip each gradient separately to a maximum norm of 0.1 0.1 times the mean candidate latent norm at the first update. After clipping, we multiply the reward gradient by 0.5 + 1.5 ​ ( s − 1 ) / ( T − 1 ) 0.5+1.5(s-1)/(T-1) and subtract the sum of the two gradients from the latent. We hold the pair weights q i ​ q j q_{i}q_{j} fixed when differentiating the diversity penalty.

For these generated images to be useful, each one must reflect the user’s preferences, measured by a learned reward, and differ visually from the others to maintain diversity. Existing methods are limited: they either address reward and diversity separately or combine them in one aggregate score, enabling high diversity to offset low rewards. In this paper, we address these limitations by formulating generation as satisficing : every image (candidate) must satisfy a reward floor and the batch of images must satisfy a diversity cutoff. The reward floor controls the balance between worst-candidate reward and batch diversity; we show that varying this floor defines a Pareto frontier. To traverse this frontier, we introduce SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method. SatisDive uses a batch-relative reward cutoff to distinguish lower- from higher-reward candidates, emphasizing reward improvement for candidates below the cutoff and diversity among candidates above it. On Pick-a-Pic, at matched DreamSim, SatisDive improves worst-candidate reward over FK steering by up to 0.43 0.43 with FLUX.1-dev as the base model and HPSv3 as the reward, and by up to 0.70 0.70 with SANA-1.6B as the base model and ImageReward as the reward. More broadly, across their overlapping DreamSim ranges, SatisDive’s satisfaction–diversity curve Pareto-dominates FK steering’s curve in each setting. Code: https://github.com/UCF-CRCV/SatisDive 1 Introduction An important goal of text-to-image generation is to give users a choice among several high-quality candidate images. For example, a user creating a poster illustration may compare images generated from the same prompt, choosing the lighting, background, or composition that best fits the poster. Recent inference-time methods increase diversity ( Singh et al., 2024 ) to provide a wider range of options, maximize a learned reward ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) to align generated images with user preferences, or select images by maximizing a linear combination of total image reward and batch diversity ( Parmar et al., 2026 ) . However, these approaches can still limit the user’s viable choices. Firstly, reward-steering methods can concentrate sampling on higher-reward images, making the returned images visually similar ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Shekhar et al., 2026 ) . Secondly, reward-free diversity methods make generated images more visually different, but do not explicitly account for learned reward ( Singh et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Corso et al., 2024 ; Vinograd et al., 2026 ) . Thirdly, batch-level reward–diversity objectives ( Parmar et al., 2026 ) allow greater diversity or high rewards for other images to compensate for one image’s low reward. These limitations motivate controlling worst-image reward through a reward floor, i.e., a minimum reward level required of each candidate. As the reward floor increases, the batch can become less diverse since fewer images satisfy the floor. We show that varying the reward floor defines a Pareto frontier between worst-image reward and batch diversity, which we call the satisfaction–diversity frontier. Along this frontier, we formulate image generation as satisficing ( Simon, 1956 ) : every generated image must satisfy a reward floor, and the batch must satisfy a diversity cutoff. Once a candidate clears the reward floor, further increases in reward do not improve satisfaction. To this end, we introduce SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method. As Figure 1 shows, SatisDive generates visually distinct images above the reward floor, while FK steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ) , a strong reward-steering baseline, returns nearly identical images. Figure 1: SatisDive returns four visually distinct images above the reward floor, while FK steering returns four nearly identical images. We use the SANA-1.6B ( Xie et al., 2025 ) flow matching model with ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) reward model. On a Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) prompt depicting two colliding viruses, the minimum reward is 0.66 0.66 for FK steering and 1.25 1.25 for SatisDive, with reward floor ρ = 1.19 \rho{=}1.19 . Our objective traverses the satisfaction–diversity frontier through a per-image reward penalty and a batch-level diversity penalty. Under the satisficing formulation, a visually different but low-reward image should contribute less to batch diversity. Thus, these penalties are complementary: images with rewards below a batch-relative reward cutoff incur larger reward penalties and contribute less to the diversity penalty, and images with rewards above the cutoff incur smaller reward penalties but contribute more to the diversity penalty. Because some candidates may remain low reward throughout denoising, we introduce late-stage latent replacement, which replaces their latents with those of higher-reward candidates. Subsequent stochastic denoising and the diversity penalty allow the resulting trajectories to produce distinct images. Empirically, SatisDive improves worst-candidate reward without sacrificing batch diversity: across their overlapping DreamSim ranges, SatisDive’s worst-candidate reward is consistently higher than FK steering’s, thus our satisfaction–diversity curves Pareto-dominate FK steering’s on both FLUX and SANA. Our contributions are as follows. • We show that different reward floors define a Pareto frontier between worst-image reward and batch diversity. Under our satisficing formulation, every image must satisfy the selected reward floor, and the batch must satisfy a diversity cutoff. • We introduce SatisDive, a training-free inference-time method whose objective provably traverses this satisfaction–diversity frontier. The objective uses a batch-relative reward cutoff to emphasize reward improvement for lower-reward candidates and diversity among higher-reward candidates. • At matched DreamSim, SatisDive improves worst-image reward by up to 0.43 0.43 on FLUX and 0.70 0.70 on SANA. Our satisfaction–diversity curve Pareto-dominates the curves traced by FK steering on the FLUX.1-dev and SANA-1.6B base models. 2 Problem Formulation A rectified-flow text-to-image model ( Liu et al., 2023 ) generates an image from a prompt c c using a learned velocity field v θ ​ ( x t , t , c ) v_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c) . This formulation also covers other diffusion models such as DDPM ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , which differ in their noise schedule ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . Additional qualitative results appear in Appendix E . 5 Related Work Reward-driven sampling. Existing methods increase reward through resampling ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2023a ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Shekhar et al., 2026 ) , value-based lookahead ( Li et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) , stochastic transitions ( Holderrieth et al., 2026 ) , adaptive model evaluation ( Kim et al., 2025a ) , or noise-space optimization and regularization ( Hwang et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Eyring et al., 2024 ; Harrington et al., 2026 ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) . These methods do not explicitly optimize batch diversity and may collapse candidate lineages ( Shekhar et al., 2026 ) . CREPE ( He et al., 2026 ) uses replica exchange to preserve diversity under reward tilting (comparison in Appendix D.8 ), while SGI ( Parmar et al., 2026 ) selects a reward–diversity batch from a large candidate pool; neither imposes a reward floor on every candidate. Reward-free diversity. NegToMe ( Singh et al., 2024 ) , CNO ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , Particle Guidance ( Corso et al., 2024 ) , and EDDY ( Vinograd et al., 2026 ) repel candidates in feature or prediction space. Other methods vary conditioning, intermediate features, or initial noise ( Sadat et al., 2024 ; Yadav et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , while general guidance modifies model predictions, attention, or guidance schedules ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Ahn et al., 2024 ; Hong, 2024 ; Karras et al., 2024 ; Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2023 ) . These methods increase diversity without imposing a reward floor. Pareto and satisficing objectives. AIG ( Jena et al., 2025 ) studies average reward against distributional coverage; PROUD ( Yao et al., 2024 ) defines Pareto objectives over per-image properties; and ParetoSlider ( Golan et al., 2026 ) , constrained diffusion alignment ( Khalafi et al., 2025 ) , and SITAlign ( Chehade et al., 2025 ) optimize expected rewards. In contrast, our training-free formulation imposes a reward floor on every candidate and a diversity requirement on the batch, producing a frontier between worst-candidate reward and batch diversity. 6 Conclusion SatisDive formulates image generation as satisficing: every candidate must satisfy a reward floor, and the batch must satisfy a diversity cutoff. Varying the floor provably traces a satisfaction–diversity Pareto frontier. On FLUX.1-dev with HPSv3 and SANA-1.6B with ImageReward, SatisDive’s curves Pareto-dominate FK steering’s over their overlapping DreamSim ranges, improving worst-candidate reward at matched DreamSim by up to 0.43 0.43 and 0.70 0.70 , respectively.
